From the source: a hollow plastic tube (an air column: harmonic overtones, no cut bar tuning), struck by hand or on the floor (a long dull noise burst, no resonator). Sound design: every number
notes: Boomwhacker page (the page titled Boomwhacker; infobox H-S '413, 111.232', 'Sets of percussion tubes'; the audit corrected 413 as wrong alone, and the page gives both, so 111.232 is the idiophone half). 'A Boomwhacker is a percussion instrument in the plosive aerophone and idiophone family. They are lightweight, hollow, color-coded, plastic tubes, tuned to a musical pitch by length.'; 'Boomwhackers produce musical tones through vibrations in the instrument when struck. The pitch of the instrument is determined by the length of the tube. The longer a tube is, the lower its pitch'; 'They are most commonly hit with a hand, against the floor, or on other parts of the human body.' Range, infobox 'range = C2-G5' (the page: 'Boomwhackers are now available to span 3+1/2 chromatic octaves'; the lower octave comes from an Octavator cap). Rule 7: judgment call. The sourced traits that no entry has are a hollow plastic tube (the page's hs desc: 'the vibration of air inside the tube'), so its overtones are an open tube's whole-number series with the fundamental dominant and the second harmonic the only overtone kept, at level 0.15 (a bar's cut overtones, the 3rd of XYLOPHONE and the 4th of MARIMBA, are not a tube's), with no resonator, a short ring, and a hand or floor strike's dull noise burst. The nearest entries are xylophone (wood bar, 1 : 3, ring 0.6 s, mallet 0.1 s at 6000 Hz) and tabla dayan (a head, 1 : 2 : 3, ring 0.6 s, mallet 0.15 s at 4000 Hz). Told apart by the 1 : 2 series, a 0.35 s ring and a 0.2 s dull strike; every number is sound design (no fetched source gives one), the traits are sourced. name: gangsa
title: Balinese gangsa (pemadé)
builder: the existing struck with three partials and the mallet: struck((Partial(ratio=1.0, level=1.0, ring_seconds=3.0), Partial(ratio=1.036, level=0.8, ring_seconds=3.0), Partial(ratio=2.71, level=0.4, ring_seconds=1.2)), release=3.0, mallet=0.06, mallet_low_pass=4000.0). From the source: the two fundamentals 228 / 220 = 1.036 apart (the pair's ombak), the metal key over its own resonator (a long ring), a wooden mallet. The ratio is taken at 220 Hz, so the beating speeds up with pitch. Sound design: the 2.71 partial (GAMELAN_METALLOPHONE's, from the catalog), every level and ring. GAMELAN_METALLOPHONE's 5.15 partial is left out: struck takes three partials with a mallet noise (four sources in all), so the weakest partial does not fit
notes: Gangsa page and Gamelan gong kebyar page (the Gangsa page gives no H-S number; 111.222 is my reading of 'tuned metal bars (either iron or bronze)'). Gangsa: 'A gangsa is a type of metallophone which is used mainly in Balinese and Javanese Gamelan music in Indonesia.'; 'Each instrument consists of several tuned metal bars (either iron or bronze) each placed over an individual resonator. The bars are hit with a wooden panggul'; 'these pairs are tuned to be dissonant and create certain wavelengths of sympathetic vibrations to create a shimmering tone (see Ombak)'. Kebyar page: 'Gangsa kantilan ... its highest note being around C7. It has ten keys, and a range of two octaves'; 'Gangsa pemadé ... also have ten keys, a range of two octaves, and are played with a wooden mallet, but are exactly one octave lower than kantilan.'; 'one note on a female gangsa pemadé might be tuned to 220 Hz, while the male gangsa pemadé might be tuned slightly higher to 228 Hz.'; 'There is no standard pitch in any Balinese music.' Range derivation (the catalog row is the pemadé, as the audit's title says): kantilan's top is around C7 and it spans two octaves, so C5 to C7; the pemadé is exactly an octave lower, so C4 to C6. Approximate, as the source says ('around C7', and each ensemble is tuned to itself): nominal pitch only. Rule 7: the catalog's keyed gamelan entries (saron, gender: GAMELAN_METALLOPHONE, trough or single resonator, no beating) have no ombak. The sourced trait is the shimmer of a pair a few hertz apart: the page's own figures, 220 Hz against 228 Hz (8 Hz of beating), so a note sounds two fundamentals 228 / 220 = 1.036 apart (63 cents; the page adds that some ensembles beat faster at higher notes, which one ratio does not show). A pair is the sourced unit (each instrument is paired male and female), so a played note is the pair in unison. Concern: ombak is a property of a pair of instruments, so this models a pair as one voice

notes: Sound-alike: Gamelan gong kebyar page, 'Gangsa kantilan': 'There are four kantilan in kebyar, two male and two female.'; 'These instruments are the highest sounding in the kebyar ensemble, with its highest note being around C7. It has ten keys, and a range of two octaves, and is played with a wooden hammer.' Gangsa page: 'the smaller, higher pitched kantilan and the larger pemade'. The pemadé is the gangsa row above, an octave lower with the same ten keys, resonators and ombak pairing, so the gangsa is the nearest and a range is no sound trait ('The mallet differs in hardness depending on the instrument and its range' gives no figure). Range derivation: highest around C7, two octaves, so C5 to C7 (approximate: 'around C7'; no standard pitch in Balinese music). H-S: the page gives none; 111.222 is my reading of its bronze or metal bars (percussion plaques, as the Glockenspiel page classes a metal-bar instrument)

It is a struck idiophone consisting of several bronze or iron plates attached by strings (in Surakarta) or a single plate (in Yogyakarta)'; 'It is used to signal cues to the gamelan to begin or end pieces, or change tempo or pathet. name: lithophone
title: Lithophone
notes: Lithophone page: 'A lithophone is a musical instrument consisting of a rock or pieces of rock which are struck to produce musical notes. ... It is an idiophone comparable to instruments such as the glockenspiel, vibraphone, xylophone and marimba.' H-S 111.22: the Lithophone page: 'In the Hornbostel-Sachs classification system, lithophones are designated as '111.22' - directly-struck percussion plaques.' 'A stone marimba is configured in the same manner as the more typical wooden bar marimba. The bars are usually wide like a wooden marimba, but are thinner, which helps increase resonance. The stone marimba may or may not have resonators.' No range for the type: the page's photo caption 'Stone marimba, range C3-C5' (an instrument from the Emil Richards Collection) is one instrument, not a documented span, and no maker or museum page giving the type's span was found, so it waits for a sourced range (fix round 1). When ranged it would be a sound-alike of the glockenspiel: the page gives no overtone ratios, ring or mallet for stone (the Rock gong page: a solid rock has a metallic tone, 'playing rocks in other such states would result in a hollow and less metallic tone'), so no sourced trait builds it apart
